urban.text: Reservoirs, drainage and craft workshops reveal organized construction and production in an arid setting.

evidence.text: Built remains and regionally attributed seals answer different questions. A modern impression makes ancient carving legible but is not itself ancient.

coordination.text: Reservoirs, drains, workshops and housing connect construction with recurring urban needs. Unequal spaces do not identify every resident’s occupation or access to water.

name: Dholavira: a city built around water
geographicPrecision: Archaeological city locator. The displayed Indus seal is regional evidence, not claimed as a Dholavira find.

interval.label: c. 3000–1500 BCE
interval.note: Occupation range in the UNESCO site account; mature urban phases and individual objects have narrower dates.

question: What makes water part of a city’s design?
summary: Dholavira joined reservoirs, drainage, housing and skilled production in an arid island setting. Seasonal water had to be captured and stored; stone-built remains let us investigate how this work fitted into the city. Different sectors and workshops reveal organized activity without identifying every resident’s status. Its c. 3000–1500 BCE occupation range is wider than the dates of the regional Indus seal shown here.

sections.title: A city needs water between rains
sections.text: Khadir’s seasonal streams supplied an urban settlement in a dry setting. Reservoirs to the east and south of the citadel, together with drains, made water management part of the built city. Capture and storage address different problems: water must first reach a place where it can be held, and the store must remain usable. The remains establish investment in those tasks; they do not preserve a complete operating manual or tell us how much each household received.

sections.title: Read components before drawing a complete system
sections.text: The ASI plan’s key names a castle well, a water chute and storm-water drain, as well as East and South reservoirs. The teaching diagram keeps those components visible and distinguishes their positions around the castle. It is schematic, combines features recorded from different phases and does not draw a verified pipe or canal between every feature. In particular, a workshop explicitly labelled Stage VI should not be assigned automatically to every stage of the city.

citations.locator: PDF p. 1, components C1, C5–C7 and reservoir labels

sections.title: Makers and residents used the city too
sections.text: Bead workshops and objects of shell, stone, copper and other materials bring skilled production into the account. Making an ornament involved more than the finished object: raw material, tools and working space had to come together. Housing varied in size and quality, and distinct fortified sectors structured movement and access. Such differences support questions about inequality. They do not give us a census of occupations, a named ruler or proof that every person within one sector had the same social position.

citations.locator: Description; Brief synthesis: crafts, houses and spatial differentiation

sections.title: A radar image is a proposal to test
sections.text: In 2015 researchers surveyed ground east of the excavated East Reservoir. Their radar reflections suggested additional water-related structures, with alternative interpretations including small reservoirs and check dams. The paper says excavation is needed to confirm their existence. An inferred buried wall is therefore different evidence from an exposed reservoir. Keeping that distinction visible prevents a tidy modern diagram from making the ancient system appear more fully known than it is.

deeperReading.title: Bring household questions to public infrastructure
deeperReading.text: A reservoir is a public-scale structure, but water also enters questions about preparation, cleaning and the demands of making things. These are useful lines of inquiry, not reconstructed routines for a named Dholavira family. The site account’s residential units and workshop spaces offer starting points for investigating how activity was distributed. More detailed work would need dated domestic assemblages and evidence of access. A large store does not prove equal availability; differences among houses do not by themselves identify an exact caste, occupation or legal category. Keep the practical problem and the social question together.

deeperReading.title: A regional seal cannot name this city’s government
deeperReading.text: The Met seal and its modern impression belong to the wider Indus world. Their signs have not been securely deciphered, and this object is not identified as a Dholavira find. Its material and carved surface support close looking at manufacture; they do not translate the institutions that maintained the reservoirs. The modern impression is also a separate act of reproduction. Compare the two surfaces to see reversal, then ask which claim needs context beyond the image. Architecture, survey and seals become stronger evidence when their distinct provenances remain visible.

familyActivity.title: Sort what is found from what is proposed
steps: Find the well, East Reservoir and South reservoirs in the schematic. Name two different jobs water structures could perform.
Find the dashed box east of the reservoir. Read why radar interpretations are shown differently.
Complete two sentences: “The exposed reservoir shows…” and “We would need excavation to test…”
familyActivity.explanation: The solid components come from the site record; the dashed box identifies a research area, not confirmed reservoir outlines. The diagram has no scale and does not show all structures operating at once.

evidenceReading.title: Three records, three different kinds of knowledge
evidenceReading.introduction: These are source paraphrases and diagram conventions, not an ancient description of the city.

items.label: A labelled plan is a composite record
items.text: The ASI key lists the castle well and drain, reservoirs, and a bead workshop attributed to Stage VI.
items.interpretation: Use the labels to identify components. Their appearance on one modern sheet does not establish contemporaneity, flow rates or a single construction event.

items.label: Chronologies have different endpoints
items.text: UNESCO uses c. 3000–1500 BCE for occupation; the radar paper’s introduction gives c. 3000–1700 BCE.
items.interpretation: The original dossier range remains intact. The difference is recorded rather than silently reconciled into an exact abandonment year.

review.reviewer: Codex source consultation and self-review; not independent historian approval
review.scope: Bounded early-city teaching account with main/deeper reading, source interpretation, reference chronology and an original explanatory diagram.
limitations: The ASI plan’s component key was consulted as indexed text; a full-resolution plan was not visually available.
Detailed household routines, water allocation and phased reservoir operation remain research gaps.
The regional seal is not assigned a Dholavira findspot.
